question: Match the following parties with their reserved symbols and choose the INCORRECT one among the following:
solution_text:
The correct answer is All India Trinamool Congress – Sickle.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The pair "All India Trinamool Congress – Sickle" is INCORRECT. The reserved symbol of the All India Trinamool Congress (AITC) is "Flowers and Grass" (Jora Ghas Phul), not the sickle. (तृणमूल कांग्रेस — जोड़ा घास फूल)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Correct symbol pairs: National People's Party – Book; Bahujan Samaj Party – Elephant; Nationalist Congress Party – Clock; BJP – Lotus; INC – Hand; AAP – Broom; CPI(M) – Hammer, Sickle and Star.

• Election symbols are allotted by the Election Commission of India under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968.

NOTE

• The AITC was founded by Mamata Banerjee in 1998; the National People's Party (Meghalaya) was the first party from the North-East to get national party status (2019).

question: What do you call the body cavity that is lined by mesoderm?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Coelom.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The "coelom" is the body cavity that is lined by the mesoderm (the middle germinal layer). It is the space between the body wall and the gut in which internal organs are accommodated. (देहगुहा — सीलोम)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Animals with a true coelom are called coelomates (e.g., annelids, chordates); those without are acoelomates (e.g., flatworms); with a false coelom — pseudocoelomates (e.g., roundworms/Aschelminthes).

• Diploblastic animals have two germ layers (ectoderm and endoderm, e.g., Hydra); triploblastic animals have three (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm).

NOTE

• Radial symmetry (body divisible into equal halves through any central plane) is seen in coelenterates and echinoderm adults; humans show bilateral symmetry.

question: With reference to provinces under Mauryan dynasty, which of the following pairs is correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Prachyapatha (East) - Toshali.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Under the Mauryan Empire, the eastern province "Prachyapatha" had its capital at "Toshali" (in Kalinga, present-day Odisha). This pair is correctly matched. (प्राच्यपथ — तोशाली)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• The Mauryan provinces and their capitals were:

◦ Uttarapatha (North) – Taxila

◦ Dakshinapatha (South) – Suvarnagiri

◦ Avantiratha (West) – Ujjain

◦ Prachyapatha (East) – Toshali

◦ Central province — capital Pataliputra (the imperial capital).

• Hence Options 1, 2 and 3 have swapped/wrong capitals.

NOTE

• The Mauryan dynasty was founded by Chandragupta Maurya (321 BCE) with the help of Chanakya (Kautilya), author of the Arthashastra. Ashoka's Kalinga War (261 BCE) took place near Toshali/Dhauli.

question:
Meher had two large chunks of coal. She set fire to the first chunk and broke the second one into pieces. Help Meher understand what kind of changes happened to the two chunks of coal at the end of the activity by choosing all the applicable statements.

A. Both chunks of coal underwent physical changes only.

B. The changes were reversible for the first chunk of coal only.

C. Only physical changes took place for the second chunk of coal.

D. Both chunks of coal underwent chemical changes only.

E. The first case is an example of chemical changes.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only C and E.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Burning the first chunk of coal is a chemical change — a new substance (ash, CO₂) is formed and the change is irreversible. So statement E is correct.

• Breaking the second chunk into pieces is a physical change — only the size/shape changes; no new substance is formed. So statement C is correct.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Statement A is wrong because burning is a chemical (not physical) change.

• Statement B is wrong because burning is irreversible, not reversible.

• Statement D is wrong because breaking coal into pieces is not a chemical change.

NOTE

• Physical change: no new substance, usually reversible (melting of ice, breaking of chalk). Chemical change: new substance formed, generally irreversible (burning, rusting, curdling of milk, digestion).

question: As per the 2011 census, which of the following union territories had the lowest population?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lakshadweep.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• As per the Census 2011, "Lakshadweep" had the lowest population among the union territories (about 64,473). It is also the smallest UT in area (about 32 sq km). (लक्षद्वीप — सबसे कम जनसंख्या)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Approximate 2011 populations: Lakshadweep ~64,000; Daman and Diu ~2.43 lakh; Andaman and Nicobar Islands ~3.8 lakh; Puducherry ~12.5 lakh; Chandigarh ~10.5 lakh; Delhi ~1.68 crore (highest among UTs).

• Lakshadweep is a group of coral islands in the Arabian Sea; its capital is Kavaratti.

NOTE

• Census 2011 was the 15th census of India (7th after independence); Census Commissioner — C. Chandramouli. Least populous state: Sikkim; most populous state: Uttar Pradesh.

question: With which of the following organisations was Henry Louis Vivian Derozio, a teacher of Hindu College of Calcutta, associated?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Young Bengal Movement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Henry Louis Vivian Derozio, a young Anglo-Indian teacher at the Hindu College, Calcutta, founded and inspired the "Young Bengal Movement" (his radical followers were called Derozians). He encouraged students to think freely and question orthodoxy. (यंग बंगाल आंदोलन — डेरोज़ियो)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Paramahansa Mandali (1849, Maharashtra) — a secret socio-religious reform society founded by Durgaram Mehtaji and others.

• Sree Narayana Dharma Paripalana (SNDP) Yogam (1903, Kerala) — founded in association with Sri Narayana Guru, who gave the message "One caste, one religion, one God for man".

• Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha (1851) — a Parsi reform association founded by Naoroji Furdonji, Dadabhai Naoroji and S. S. Bengalee.

NOTE

• Derozio died young in 1831 at the age of 22. The Hindu College, Calcutta (founded 1817), later became Presidency College.

question: In which of the following empires of South India was the Kamalapuram tank built in the 15th century?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vijayanagara.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The "Kamalapuram tank" was built in the 15th century in the Vijayanagara Empire (near Hampi, Karnataka). It supplied water to the fields and to the "royal centre" of the capital city. (कमलापुरम तालाब — विजयनगर साम्राज्य)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• The Vijayanagara Empire (1336 CE) was founded by Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty; its capital Hampi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

• The empire was famous for irrigation works (tanks, canals on the Tungabhadra), the Virupaksha temple and the Vitthala temple with its stone chariot.

• Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529) of the Tuluva dynasty was its greatest ruler; he wrote Amuktamalyada.

NOTE

• Bidar and Bijapur were Deccan (Bahmani successor) sultanates; the Cholas ruled much earlier (9th–13th centuries) from Thanjavur.

question: In May 2023, who was sworn in as the new Central Vigilance Commissioner of India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is PK Srivastava.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In May 2023, Praveen Kumar (PK) Srivastava was sworn in as the Central Vigilance Commissioner (CVC) of India. The oath was administered by President Droupadi Murmu. (केंद्रीय सतर्कता आयुक्त — पी.के. श्रीवास्तव)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• The Central Vigilance Commission was set up in 1964 on the recommendation of the Santhanam Committee; it got statutory status by the CVC Act, 2003.

• The CVC consists of a Central Vigilance Commissioner and up to two Vigilance Commissioners, appointed by the President on the recommendation of a committee of the PM, Home Minister and Leader of Opposition (Lok Sabha).

• Suresh N Patel was the previous CVC; G C Murmu is associated with the office of Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG).

NOTE

• The CVC is the apex integrity institution to check corruption in central government organisations; term of office — 4 years or 65 years of age, whichever is earlier.

question: Gangubai Hangal, a renowned Indian music personality, is recognised for her contributions in which of the following fields?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Hindustani Classical Music.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Gangubai Hangal (1913–2009) was a legendary vocalist of "Hindustani Classical Music", belonging to the Kirana Gharana. She was famous for her powerful renditions of khayal. (गंगूबाई हंगल — हिंदुस्तानी शास्त्रीय संगीत, किराना घराना)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• She hailed from Dharwad, Karnataka, and was a disciple of Sawai Gandharva (guru also of Bhimsen Joshi).

• Honours: Padma Bhushan (1971) and Padma Vibhushan (2002), besides the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award.

NOTE

• Indian classical music has two major systems: Hindustani (North India — khayal, dhrupad, thumri) and Carnatic (South India — kriti). Famous Kirana Gharana artists: Abdul Karim Khan, Sawai Gandharva, Bhimsen Joshi, Gangubai Hangal.

question: On 19 July 2023, who was appointed as the 25th Director General of the Indian Coast Guard?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rakesh Pal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• On 19 July 2023, Rakesh Pal was appointed as the 25th Director General of the Indian Coast Guard (ICG). (राकेश पाल — भारतीय तटरक्षक बल के 25वें महानिदेशक)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• The Indian Coast Guard was formally established in 1978 (Coast Guard Act, 1978) and functions under the Ministry of Defence; its motto is "Vayam Rakshamah" (We Protect).

• Its headquarters is in New Delhi; it protects India's maritime interests, enforces maritime law and conducts search-and-rescue operations.

• K Natarajan was an earlier DG of the Coast Guard.

NOTE

• The ICG is the fourth armed force of India (after Army, Navy, Air Force) and works closely with the Indian Navy for coastal security.

question: Which of the following National Waterways (NW) is associated with the Udyogamandal and the Champakkara canals?
solution_text:
The correct answer is NW-3.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "National Waterway-3 (NW-3)", the West Coast Canal in Kerala (Kottapuram to Kollam), includes the Udyogamandal canal and the Champakkara canal. It was declared a national waterway in 1993. (राष्ट्रीय जलमार्ग-3 — केरल)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Major National Waterways:

◦ NW-1 — Ganga (Prayagraj–Haldia, 1,620 km, the longest).

◦ NW-2 — Brahmaputra (Sadiya–Dhubri).

◦ NW-3 — West Coast Canal, Kerala (Kottapuram–Kollam) with Udyogamandal and Champakkara canals.

◦ NW-4 — Godavari–Krishna canal system; NW-5 — Brahmani–East Coast Canal (Odisha).

• Waterways are managed by the Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI), established in 1986.

NOTE

• NW-3 is India's first waterway with all-time navigability; the National Waterways Act, 2016 declared a total of 111 National Waterways.

question: In basketball, how many points are awarded when a basket is scored from outside the 6.25-metre line?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Three points.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In basketball, a basket scored from outside the 6.25-metre (three-point) line earns "three points". Baskets scored inside the line earn two points. (तीन अंक — थ्री-पॉइंट लाइन के बाहर से)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• A free throw (after a foul) earns one point; a field goal inside the arc earns two points.

• A basketball team has 5 players on court; the game was invented by James Naismith (1891) in the USA.

• Basketball is governed internationally by FIBA (International Basketball Federation).

NOTE

• FIBA later moved the three-point arc to 6.75 m (NBA: 7.24 m), but the classic distance asked in exams is 6.25 m. Famous terms: dribble, dunk, rebound, layup.

question: In which of the following states is the Mamallapuram Utsav celebrated?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Tamil Nadu.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The "Mamallapuram Utsav" (Mamallapuram/Mahabalipuram Dance Festival) is celebrated in Tamil Nadu, at the historic town of Mamallapuram near Chennai, against the backdrop of the Pallava rock-cut monuments. (मामल्लपुरम उत्सव — तमिलनाडु)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram) was a port city of the Pallava dynasty, developed by king Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla).

• Its Group of Monuments — the Shore Temple, Pancha Rathas, Arjuna's Penance/Descent of the Ganges — is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1984).

• Classical dances like Bharatanatyam, Kuchipudi, Kathak and Odissi are performed at the festival.

NOTE

• Other famous dance festivals: Khajuraho (Madhya Pradesh), Konark (Odisha), Ellora (Maharashtra), Pattadakal (Chalukya) Utsav (Karnataka).

question: Most of the Harappan sites are primarily divided into _________ parts.
solution_text:
The correct answer is two.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Most Harappan (Indus Valley) cities were divided into "two" parts — the Citadel (a smaller, raised western part with important buildings) and the Lower Town (a larger, lower eastern part where common people lived). (दो भाग — दुर्ग और निचला नगर)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• The Citadel contained structures like the Great Bath and Granary (at Mohenjo-daro); the Lower Town had residential houses laid out on a grid pattern.

• Harappan towns had burnt-brick buildings, covered drains and standardised weights and measures.

• The civilisation flourished around 2600–1900 BCE; major sites: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Lothal, Kalibangan, Rakhigarhi.

NOTE

• Exception: Dholavira (Gujarat) was divided into three parts. Harappa was excavated by Daya Ram Sahni (1921) and Mohenjo-daro by R. D. Banerji (1922).

question: What is the role of a commercial bank in the economy?
option_2: To set interest rates for the entire banking system
option_3: To provide financial services, such as accepting deposits, lending money and facilitating payments
solution_text:
The correct answer is To provide financial services, such as accepting deposits, lending money and facilitating payments.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "commercial bank" is a financial institution whose primary role is to accept deposits from the public, lend money (loans/advances) and facilitate payments (cheques, drafts, digital transfers). It works for profit. (वाणिज्यिक बैंक — जमा स्वीकारना, ऋण देना, भुगतान सुविधा)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Printing/issuing currency, setting policy interest rates (repo, reverse repo, bank rate) and regulating money supply are functions of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) — the central bank, established in 1935 and nationalised in 1949.

• Commercial banks also perform agency functions (collecting cheques, paying bills) and general utility functions (lockers, forex).

NOTE

• Types of commercial banks in India: public sector (SBI, PNB), private sector (HDFC, ICICI), foreign banks, Regional Rural Banks. Banks create credit through the money multiplier process.

question: Which of the following is NOT considered as a Fundamental Duty?
option_1: To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture
option_3: To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
option_4: To develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform
solution_text:
The correct answer is To uphold and protect secularism.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "To uphold and protect secularism" is NOT listed as a Fundamental Duty in Article 51A of the Constitution. The other three options are Fundamental Duties. (मौलिक कर्तव्य नहीं)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Fundamental Duties (Article 51A, Part IV-A) were added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee — originally 10 duties; the 11th (education of children aged 6–14) was added by the 86th Amendment, 2002.

• Duties include: to abide by the Constitution and respect the National Flag and Anthem; to protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; to preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture; to develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform; to protect the natural environment.

• They are borrowed from the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR and are non-justiciable.

NOTE

• "Secularism" appears in the Preamble (added by the 42nd Amendment) but not as a Fundamental Duty.

question: Scissor style and Western Roll are the techniques used in:
solution_text:
The correct answer is high jump.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Scissors style" and "Western Roll" are jumping techniques used in the "high jump" event of athletics. (हाई जंप की तकनीकें)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Other high-jump techniques: Straddle, Eastern cut-off and the modern "Fosbury Flop" (introduced by Dick Fosbury, 1968 Mexico Olympics), in which the jumper goes over the bar back-first.

• Long jump techniques: hang, hitch-kick, sail; triple jump = hop, step and jump; pole vault uses a flexible pole to clear the bar.

NOTE

• High jump is a field event; the bar is raised progressively and a jumper is eliminated after three consecutive failures. World-famous high jumpers: Javier Sotomayor (2.45 m world record), Mutaz Barshim.

question: Large tidal waves caused by an underwater earthquake or volcanic eruption are known as a _________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is tsunami.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Large sea waves caused by an underwater earthquake, volcanic eruption or landslide are called a "tsunami" (a Japanese word meaning "harbour wave"). (सुनामी)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• In deep ocean, tsunami waves travel very fast (700–800 km/h) with a small height; near the coast they slow down and rise to devastating heights.

• The 26 December 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami (caused by an earthquake off Sumatra) severely hit the Indian coast and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands.

• India's tsunami early-warning centre (ITEWC) is at INCOIS, Hyderabad.

NOTE

• Hurricane (Atlantic), typhoon (western Pacific) and cyclone (Indian Ocean) are tropical storms — names differ by region; a tornado is a violent rotating column of air over land. None of these is caused by undersea earthquakes.

question: As a part of the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922, the angry peasants had set ablaze the police station of which place?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chauri Chaura.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• On 5 February 1922, during the Non-Cooperation Movement, angry peasants set fire to the police station at "Chauri Chaura" (Gorakhpur district, Uttar Pradesh), killing about 22 policemen. (चौरी-चौरा कांड — 1922)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Shocked by the violence, Mahatma Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement on 12 February 1922 (Bardoli resolution).

• The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) was launched on the issues of the Khilafat wrong, Punjab (Jallianwala Bagh) wrong and Swaraj.

• Kakori (UP) is linked to the Kakori train action, 1925 (HRA revolutionaries); Dandi (Gujarat) to the Salt March, 1930.

NOTE

• After withdrawal of the movement, leaders like C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party (1923) to enter legislative councils.

question: Which of the following rivers flows north of the Tropic of Cancer in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Yamuna.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The "Yamuna" flows north of the Tropic of Cancer (23°30′ N). It rises from the Yamunotri glacier (Uttarakhand) and joins the Ganga at Prayagraj — its entire course lies in northern India. (यमुना — कर्क रेखा के उत्तर में)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• The Mahanadi (Chhattisgarh–Odisha), Tapi (MP–Maharashtra–Gujarat, west-flowing) and Penganga (a tributary of the Wardha/Godavari system in Maharashtra) all flow south of the Tropic of Cancer, in peninsular India.

• The Tropic of Cancer passes through 8 Indian states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram.

• Main tributaries of the Yamuna: Chambal, Betwa, Ken, Sind (right) and Hindon (left).

NOTE

• The Yamuna is the longest tributary of the Ganga; Delhi, Mathura and Agra are situated on its banks.

question: The Huttari dance, observed as an annual tradition, is a leisurely performance that takes place during the harvesting season in _____________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Karnataka.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The "Huttari dance" is performed annually during the harvest season in the Kodagu (Coorg) region of Karnataka. "Huttari" means "new rice crop", and the festival celebrates the first harvest of paddy. (हुत्तरी नृत्य — कर्नाटक, कोडगु)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Other folk dances of Karnataka: Yakshagana (dance-drama), Dollu Kunitha (drum dance), Veeragase and Kamsale.

• Harvest festivals of India: Makar Sankranti (north India), Pongal (Tamil Nadu), Onam (Kerala), Baisakhi (Punjab), Nuakhai (Odisha), Huttari (Kodagu, Karnataka).

NOTE

• Kodagu (Coorg) is also famous for coffee cultivation and the river Kaveri originates there at Talakaveri.

question: What is the study of the interactions between living organisms and their environment called?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ecology.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Ecology" is the branch of science that studies the interactions between living organisms and their environment (both living/biotic and non-living/abiotic components). (पारिस्थितिकी)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• The term "ecology" (Oekologie) was coined by the German biologist Ernst Haeckel (1866).

• Levels of ecological organisation: organism → population → community → ecosystem → biome → biosphere.

• The term "ecosystem" was given by A. G. Tansley (1935).

• Biology is the study of life in general; Geology — the Earth's structure and rocks; Chemistry — matter and its reactions.

NOTE

• "Father of Indian Ecology" — Ramdeo Misra. Ecology forms the basis of environmental studies asked widely in SSC exams (food chains, trophic levels, biogeochemical cycles).

question: If labour is employed in a job but is not actually utilised for the production of goods and services, it is known as:
solution_text:
The correct answer is disguised unemployment.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Disguised unemployment" occurs when people appear to be employed but their contribution to production is nil or negligible — i.e., labour is engaged in a job but not actually utilised. Removing such workers would not reduce total output (their marginal productivity is zero). (प्रच्छन्न बेरोज़गारी)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Disguised unemployment is most common in the Indian agricultural sector, where an entire family may work on a field that needs fewer hands.

• Seasonal unemployment — people are without work during certain seasons (e.g., farm labourers after harvest).

• Educated unemployment — educated youth unable to find suitable jobs (mainly urban).

• Urban unemployment — general unemployment in cities (industrial/educated).

NOTE

• Other types: structural, frictional, cyclical and technological unemployment. In India, unemployment data is published by the NSSO/PLFS (Periodic Labour Force Survey).

question: Which Kuchipudi dancer received National Nritya Shiromani Award 2022?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Aparna Satheesan.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Aparna Satheesan, a renowned Kuchipudi dancer, received the "National Nritya Shiromani Award 2022" for her contribution to Indian classical dance. (कुचिपुड़ी नृत्यांगना — अपर्णा सतीशन)

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• The Nritya Shiromani award is presented at the Cuttack Mahotsav (Odisha) to honour excellence in dance.

• Kuchipudi is the classical dance form of Andhra Pradesh, which originated in the village of Kuchipudi (Krishna district); Siddhendra Yogi is regarded as its founder.

• A unique feature of Kuchipudi is the Tarangam, in which the dancer performs on the rim of a brass plate.

NOTE

• The eight classical dances of India: Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathak (UP), Kathakali & Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur), Sattriya (Assam).

question: The God of Small Things is a novel authored by whom among the following authors?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Arundhati Roy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "The God of Small Things" (1997) is a famous novel by the Indian author Arundhati Roy. It won the Booker Prize in 1997, making her the first Indian woman to win the award. (अरुंधति रॉय — 'द गॉड ऑफ स्मॉल थिंग्स')

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• The novel is set in Ayemenem (Kerala) and tells the story of the twins Rahel and Estha.

• Arundhati Roy's other major work: The Ministry of Utmost Happiness (2017).

• Rohinton Mistry — "A Fine Balance", "Such a Long Journey"; Shashi Tharoor — "The Great Indian Novel", "An Era of Darkness"; "Fakira" is not an author of this novel.

NOTE

• Indian Booker winners: Arundhati Roy (1997), Kiran Desai (2006 — The Inheritance of Loss), Aravind Adiga (2008 — The White Tiger); Geetanjali Shree won the International Booker 2022 for "Tomb of Sand".
